claims.text: The unmodified (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy has a large applied-field and pressure-induced caloric response.
The unmodified alloy has poor fracture resistance and tends to crack.
Adding approximately 1–3 at% boron during synthesis will induce in-situ high-entropy boride precipitation.
The boride precipitates will be uniformly dispersed at grain boundaries and within the alloy matrix.
High-entropy transition-metal borides can exhibit high strength and phase stability under extreme pressure and temperature conditions.
The proposed boride nanoprecipitates will pin dislocations in the modified alloy.
The proposed boride nanoprecipitates will retard crack initiation and propagation.
Boride precipitation will increase the alloy's compressive strength and toughness.
The precipitates will be chemically and structurally compatible with the martensitic or magnetostructural transformation responsible for the caloric effect.
The modified alloy could achieve at least a 50% increase in compressive strength and crack resistance relative to the untreated alloy.
The modified alloy's applied-field or pressure-induced caloric response will remain within 10% of the baseline response.
The hypothesis applies only when magnetic field, pressure, and temperature do not trigger additional phase instabilities.
Boron content and processing must be controlled so that precipitate formation does not interfere with the caloric transformation.
Mechanical performance is proposed to be assessed under compressive loading up to approximately 200 MPa.
A failure to obtain more than approximately 25% improvement in mechanical robustness would falsify the hypothesis.
A degradation of caloric response by more than approximately 10% would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The predicted mechanical improvement is at least 50%, but the experiment only falsifies improvements of 25% or less. An outcome between 25% and 50% would fail the stated prediction without satisfying the stated falsification rule.
